Order 
The present first appeal under Section 96 of the Civil Procedure Code has been filed challenging the order dated 31.08.1995 whereby the preliminary issue No.1 in respect of limitation and the suit being time barred has been decided in favor of the defendants and consequently, the suit has been dismissed as time barred.

2. Learned counsel for the appellant contends that the appellant had filed a suit for specific performance of agreement dated 24.04.1988 which was executed between the plaintiff and deceased Lokesh Prasad/defendant No.1 who is now represented by respondents No.1 to 4.

It is the further case of the plaintiff that the said Lokesh Prasad died before executing sale deed in June 1988 and after death of Lokesh Prasad, a fresh agreement was executed by the defendant No.1 in favour of the appellant-plaintiff on 25.06.1988.

3. It is further contended that as per plaint averments, the agreement was dated 24.04.1988 and the plaintiff had paid Rs.2,000/- as advance of agreed consideration amount of Rs.42,000/- and the balance of Rs.40,000/- was to be 2 FA-245-1996 paid at the time of execution of sale deed.

4. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that the trial Court has erroneously held the suit to be time barred holding that the suit has been filed on 05.08.1992 which is more than 4 years after the agreement was executed on 24.04.1988 with deceased Lokesh Prasad as well as the alleged subsequent agreement dated 25.06.1988 executed with respondent No.1/defendant No.1 who is widow of Lokesh Prasad.
5. Learned counsel for the appellant has argued that the suit land was sold to defendants No.5 and 6 by different sale deeds dated 13.05.1988 and 16.04.1991.

As soon as the plaintiff came to the knowledge of the suit land having been sold to third parties by the aforesaid sale deeds, he filed the suit in question because the cause of action to file the suit arose in the year 1991 as soon as the plaintiff came to knowledge of the suit land having been sold to third parties.
It is further contended that the plaintiff was ever ready and willing to execute the sale deed upon payment of balance Rohini Prasad vs Smt. Deoki Bai & Ors.

Per contra, it is argued by learned counsel for the respondent No.5 and 6 that in the present case, the date of agreement was undisputedly 24.04.1988 and the date of filing of suit was 05.08.1992 which is undisputed.

11. It is also argued by learned counsel for respondent No.5 & 6 who are subsequent purchasers and claim to be bonafide purchasers that undisputedly the agreement was executed on 24.04.1988 and the suit has been filed in 4 FA-245-1996 August, 1992.

The time gap between filing of suit and execution of agreement is 4 years and four months and during this time lapse, even as per plaint averments, the plaintiff had not pleaded about sending any reminder or notice to the defendant No.1 or deceased Lokesh Prasad expressing his readiness or willingness to execute the sale deed.
1 2 .
It is contended that even if there is no time limit to execute the agreement, then the time limit would be three years to get specific performance of contract.
13. It is further argued that the trial Court has rightly held that the limitation to file the suit ended in the year 1991 and the suit filed in August 1992 is clearly barred by limitation.
It is further contended that no questions of facts arose which were required to be established by the plaintiff by way of evidence to explain the delay caused in filing of the plaint.

The cause of action was projected by the plaintiff to be the second sale deed dated 16.04.1991 but in fact the cause of action arose on the date of agreement itself and on expiry of 3 years of date of agreement, the limitation to file the suit came to an end in accordance with the provisions of Limitation Act.
14.
It is further argued that the trial court has rightly held that the appellant is not entitled to get benefit of Article 54 of Limitation Act (wrongly mentioned as Section 54 in the impugned order).

15. Thus, it is contended that the trial Court has not erred in deciding the preliminary issue without recording of evidence because no evidence was required to be recorded in view of the pleadings of plaintiff.

16. Heard learned counsel for the parties at length.
17.

In the present case, the agreement in question is not part of record of trhe trial Court and the same has been filed alongwith an application under 5 FA-245-1996 Order 41 Rule 27 CPC (IA No. 5653/2024).

As per this agreement, it is mentioned therein that the plaintiff has paid Rs. 2,000/- out of agreed sale consideration of Rs.
42,000/- and rest amount will be paid at the time of execution of sale deed.
18.
Even in the plaint, it has been admitted in para-7 and 14 that the plaintiff has not paid the balance consideration of Rs. 40,000/- to the defendants No. 1 to 4 till filing of suit.
There is no averment that the amount was tendered but these defendants refused to accept the amount.

sentences.text: Even if the said agreement is seen, then it is clear that the plaintiff has not performed his part of the contract, i.e. payment of entire sale consideration.
His part remains to be performed by payment of remaining sale consideration.

Reliance was placed on Article 54 of the Limitation Act to state that it would be at the sweet will of the plaintiff to file the suit for specific performance at his own sweet will and limitation will not come in way, immaterial of when he files the suit.
It was argued that the starting point of limitation would be getting knowledge of the sale deed in favor of defendants No. 5 and 6, and the date of knowledge would be a question of fact.

Article 54 is as under :-
"Article 54 of the Limitation Act:
For specific Three years The date fixed for the performance, performance or,if no such date is fixed when of a contract the plaintiff has notice that performance is refused.
20. The question of refusal to perform the contract by the defendants No. 1 to 4 would arise only when the plaintiff pays the balance consideration.

There is no averment in the plaint that any notice was given to the defendants 1 6 FA-245-1996 to 4 to accept the balance consideration and even then they refused to accept the consideration and execute the sale deed.
Since there is no assertion of such fact of issuing any notice to the defendants No. 1 to 4 in the plaint, there cannot be evidence to that effect.

21. A heavy reliance was placed by the appellant on the judgement in case of Bheru Chandani &
another Vs. Shivkumar Gupta & Others 2019 (13) SCC 372 to submit that the plaintiff could file suit even after 25 years when no time was fixed for execution of the sale deed.

the said case does not help the case of the appellant because in the aforesaid case, the entire sale consideration was paid by the plaintiff and only the part of the defendant remained to be performed.
22. However, in the present case, the plaintiff having paid hardly 5% of the consideration amount.
Is stressing that it is his option and he can execute the sale deed and file suit at his own will at any point of time.
Thus, the appellant is not covered by Article 54 and this plea would be inequitable to the defendants No. 1 to 4 also.

23. Furthermore, there is no averment in the plaint that the plaintiff at any point of time ever,
expressed his willingness to execute the sale deed by paying the remaining sale consideration.

As per Section 16 of the Specific Relief Act 1963, the following is provided :-
16.

24. As per Explanation (ii) of the said Act, the plaintiff must aver performance of, or readiness and willingness to perform, the contract according to its true construction.
In the present case, there is no notice in terms of section 16 of the Act of 1963, nor pleading regarding having sent any notice.

sentences.text: From perusal of the plaint on the record it, transpires that there is a statement in Paragraph No. 6 that till the month of October, 1980, the original respondent (since deceased) and her husband (now, as Legal Representative) had asked the appellants to execute the Sale Deed and then an eviction notice was served on the original respondent (since deceased) and her husband (now, as Legal Representative) and his brother.
It has further been stated that this was after the respondents asked the appellants to execute the Sale Deed within 15 days after taking permission.

Thus,
nowhere it has been even indicated, in clear terms, that the respondents were ready and willing to pay the balance amount and get the Sale Deed executed in their favour.

In view thereof, from their own pleadings in the plaint, even after five and a half years, there being no averment that the respondents were ready and willing to perform their obligations under the ATS and pay the balance/remaining amount is enough for the suit of the respondents to be dismissed on the ground of limitation alone.
The ATS is dated 31.07.1975 and the suit was filed on 01.01.1981.

The 8 FA-245-1996 limitation for filing a suit for specific performance, as per Article 54 of the Schedule to The Limitation Act, 1963 is 3 years 'from the date fixed for performance or if no such date is fixed, when the plaintiff has notice that the performance is refused.'

In Ghewarchand v. Mahendra Singh, (2018) 10 SCC 588, it was observed that when deciding upon the question of limitation, it is mainly required to see the plaint allegations and how the plaintiff has pleaded the accrual of cause of action for filing of the suit.

Apropos limitation, this Court observed, in Basawaraj v. Land Acquisition Officer, (2013) 14 SCC 81 as under:
'12.

sentences.text: It is a settled legal proposition that law of limitation may harshly affect a particular party but it has to be applied with all its rigour when the statute so prescribes.
The court has no power to extend the period of limitation on equitable grounds.
"A result flowing from a statutory provision is never an evil.
A court has no power to ignore that provision to relieve what it considers a distress resulting from its operation."
The statutory provision may cause hardship or inconvenience to a Rohini Prasad vs Smt. Deoki Bai & Ors.

particular party but the court has no choice but to enforce it giving full effect to the same.
The legal maxim dura lex sed lex which means "the law is hard but it is the law", stands attracted in such a situation.

It has consistently been held that,
"inconvenience is not" a decisive factor to be considered while interpreting a statute.
13.
The statute of limitation is founded on public policy, its aim being to secure peace in the community, to suppress fraud and perjury, to quicken diligence and to prevent oppression.
It seeks to bury all acts of the past which have not been agitated unexplainably and have from lapse of time become stale.

According to Halsbury's Laws of England, Vol. 28, p. 266:
"605. Policy of the Limitation Acts.-- The courts have expressed at least three differing reasons supporting the existence of statutes of limitations namely, (1) that long dormant claims have more of cruelty than justice in them, (2) that a defendant might have lost the 9 FA-245-1996 evidence to disprove a stale claim, and (3) that persons with good causes of actions should pursue them with reasonable diligence."

An unlimited limitation would lead to a sense of insecurity and uncertainty, and therefore,
limitation prevents disturbance or deprivation of what may have been acquired in equity and justice by long enjoyment or what may have been lost by a party's own inaction, negligence or laches.

(See Popat and Kotecha Property v. SBI Staff Assn. [(2005) 7 SCC 510], Rajender Singh v. Santa Singh [(1973) 2 SCC 705 : AIR 1973 SC 2537] and Pundlik Jalam Patil v. Jalgaon Medium Project [(2008)
17 SCC 448 : (2009) 5 SCC (Civ) 907].)'
26.

In Prem Chand Vijay Kumar vs Yashpal Singh And Anr 2005 (6) SCC 514 , it has been held that when limitation is a pure question of law and from the pleadings itself it is apparent that that the suit is barred by limitation, then the same can be decided at the outset even without a plea.

28. The appeal fails and is dismissed.
